title: Exact Microscopic One-Body Reduction in the Symmetric Exclusion Process
abstract: The symmetric exclusion process (SEP) is a paradigmatic model of interacting particle transport. Its current--density correlations are governed by an infinite many-body hierarchy of equations. Only recently, this hierarchy was found to collapse at large scales onto a single closed equation. Is this remarkable simplification created by coarse graining, or does it reflect a deeper property already present in the microscopic dynamics? Here we show that the second scenario is realized. At arbitrary time on the lattice, the entire hierarchy collapses onto a single linear equation which is exactly equivalent to a persistence problem for a single auxiliary random walker. Thus an interacting many-body problem reduces exactly to a genuine one-body problem before any scaling limit is taken. This reduction determines the complete finite-time correlation profile, including during nonequilibrium relaxation. More broadly, the microscopic operator uncovered here opens a route to more general correlation functions in the SEP, and may point to a general organizing principle for nonequilibrium interacting particle systems.
summary: This work solves a major problem in non-equilibrium statistical mechanics by showing that the complex, many-body correlation dynamics of the Symmetric Exclusion Process (SEP) simplify exactly. The infinite hierarchy of equations collapses onto a single, linear equation equivalent to a single random walker's persistence problem. This establishes a fundamental, microscopic one-body description for the system's behavior.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of determining the correlation profile in the Symmetric Exclusion Process (SEP), which is governed by an intractable, infinite many-body hierarchy of equations.
main_result: They prove that the complex many-body problem reduces exactly to a simple, genuine one-body problem equivalent to a persistence problem for a single auxiliary random walker, even at finite time.
method: The authors employ advanced techniques involving the stirring representation, Bethe-ansatz calculations, and the use of Poisson transforms to derive a closed, linear equation for the correlation profile.
model_or_system: The system studied is the Symmetric Exclusion Process (SEP), a fundamental model for interacting particle transport on a lattice where particles undergo symmetric random walks subject to hard-core exclusion.
key_observables: The correlation profile $\omega_r(t; \lambda)$ and the $n$-particle propagators $\langle \eta_{r_1}(t) \cdots \eta_{r_n}(t) angle$.
important_parameters: Time ($t$), spatial lattice positions ($r$), and the coupling parameter $\lambda$. The analysis distinguishes between finite-time microscopic regimes and large-scale diffusive limits.
main_assumptions: The derivation relies on extending the microscopic Bethe-ansatz calculation and involves complex mathematical manipulations like contour deformations and expansions in the large-scale limit.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the SEP as a stirring process, showing how the particle configuration is derived from the initial labeling of particles.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first identifying the many-body hierarchy, then developing the microscopic tools (Bethe ansatz, determinantal representations) to derive a closed, linear equation, and finally demonstrating that this equation is equivalent to a single random walker's persistence problem.
why_interesting: The finding that a complex, interacting many-body system reduces exactly to a one-body problem before any scaling limit is taken provides a powerful, general organizing principle for understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in interacting particle systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Representation of the SEP as a stirring process [3]. At random times, picked with unit rate, two neighboring integers are exchanged (red arrows). A configuration of the SEP is obtained by filling the sites hosting a label that was initially occupied by a particle (blue). Note that exchanging the labels of two occupied sites yield the same SEP configuration.
